## Active

### D-676 — The webhook adapter becomes a bidirectional port

> _2026-10-29 · realm/blong-chat · active_

The adapter at core/blong-gogo/src/adapter/server/webhook.ts posts only: it resolves a descriptor
and hands it to got. blong-chat needs the opposite direction, so the port gains a listening half
modelled on ut-port-webhook (a fastify route per configured path, raw body kept for signature
checks, identity then message handler hooks, and a reply shaped by a server hook with reply/server
modes). The platform adapters (slack, viber) extend this port rather than the RPC gateway, because a
webhook request cannot carry a JWT and its signature must be checked over the raw bytes before any
schema parses them.

### D-677 — blong-chat is stateless in its first pass, with named seams for state

> _2026-10-29 · realm/blong-chat · active_

Conversation state would cost a database, a schema, seeds and model pages before a single message is
exchanged, so the first pass keeps credentials in the rc file and Secrets and holds pending
interactive prompts in memory, lost on restart. The two places state would enter are isolated behind
library functions (an account registry that reads the accounts map, and a pending prompt store with
add, get and remove) so a later stateful implementation replaces those functions rather than the
orchestrators. The UT appId and clientId path parameters are kept in the listener path because they
are what names an account in an existing Slacks and Viber bot configuration.

### D-678 — Interactive prompts answer twice: a promise and an event

> _2026-10-29 · realm/blong-chat · active_

A caller replacing the askQuestions tool wants a question to return its answer, so chatPromptAsk
dispatches the controls, parks the call on a pending prompt and resolves it when the answer arrives
or the timeout expires. A caller that cannot wait uses the same controls through chatMessageSend and
implements chatInAnswerReceive, which is also the hook the park resolves through, so the two paths
share one correlation token rather than two. The controls are canonical (choice, multiChoice, text,
confirm) and each platform maps them to what it can render: Slack gets Block Kit buttons and a modal
with checkboxes, radio buttons and a plain text input, Viber gets keyboard buttons and a plain text
reply, and a control a platform cannot render is reported as a typed error rather than silently
degraded.

### D-679 — One port per platform, accounts as a map

> _2026-10-29 · realm/blong-chat · active_

A port per account would multiply listeners, namespaces and ingress paths for a difference the
platform APIs do not have, so each platform is one port whose config carries an accounts map keyed
by the account alias. The alias, the appId and the clientId travel in the request path (the UT
shape), which is what a single Slack app configuration or Viber webhook can point at and what lets
one listener answer several bots. The map is the merge-friendly shape the guardrails ask for: an rc
file, a suite config and a Secret-backed deployment each add an account rather than replacing the
list.

### D-682 — Chat gateway methods are unauthenticated in the first pass

> _2026-10-29 · realm/blong-chat · active_

The realm carries no users, and a login realm would bring a database the stateless pass deliberately
avoids, so the chat gateway validations declare auth false and a local tool calls chat.message.send
and chat.prompt.ask with plain JSON-RPC. What protects the address is the deployment rather than the
realm: the chat host is not a portal, its ingress carries no basic or oauth2 annotations, and the
channel is the platform signature on the inbound side. A stateful pass that adds users and access
turns these routes to jwt; until then, exposing the gateway port publicly would let anybody speak as
the bot.

### D-681 — The platform API sim runs on the webhook receiver, not the OpenAPI orchestrator

> _2026-10-29 · realm/blong-chat · active_

The blong-test-sim skill prescribes orchestrator.openapi for HTTP back ends that have a spec. Slack
and Viber publish no OpenAPI document this repository carries, and the surface a chat test needs is
three endpoints whose request descriptors are the thing under test, so the sim layer runs a second
webhook adapter with listen true that answers the platform paths and asserts the descriptors it
received. The receiver being exercised in both directions is the second reason: a simulator built on
it fails when the port fails. Keeping a published document in the tree and switching to
orchestrator.openapi stays an option if the endpoint set grows.

### D-685 — The forward seam is one method with a realm default consumer

> _2026-10-29 · realm/blong-chat · active_

One setting, one default, one consumer: `chat.chatDispatch.forward` names the method an inbound
message is dispatched to, and the dispatch port's activation names `chat.in.message.ignore` until a
deployment names its own, which logs the drop and acknowledges the platform. The alternative — two
targets (`forward.message` and `forward.answer`) with the answer path falling back to a
`chatPromptNothingPending` 409 — produced a branch no valid configuration could reach (a deployment
with a message consumer but no answer consumer) and refused a click that arrived after its ask had
timed out, which a platform retries and a caller cannot undo. An unclaimed answer is now
acknowledged and settled by the port's own request log, so the fallback is gone rather than tested.

### D-687 — An account carries its API base, its public address and its consumer

> _2026-10-30 · realm/blong-chat · active_

An account is not only a token: it names the API base its calls go to (`url`), the public address it
answers on (`ngrokUrl`) and, for Slack, the app configuration token that may rewrite the app. The
base is per account because one process serves a real workspace and a simulator at the same time,
and the port's own `url` is only the fallback for an account that names none. The realm's
`chat.chatDispatch.forward` became a map for the same reason:
`{'*': 'chat.in.message.ignore', demo: 'test.chat.received'}` lets a test account feed a recorder
while the production account feeds a realm, and an account nobody maps still gets an answered,
logged drop. The listener's port stays the same in both cases — the account decides where the
conversation happens, not which socket was opened.

### D-690 — A question echoes its answer, per question and before the ask returns

> _2026-10-30 · realm/blong-chat · active_

A question echoes its answer back into the conversation by default, and the switch is per question:
`echoAnswer: false` on one `chat.prompt.ask` turns it off. Per question rather than per deployment
because one conversation usually holds both kinds — a survey whose answers nobody needs to read, and
an approval whose answer is the whole point — and a realm-wide setting would force the caller to
choose which of the two it is for everybody. The echo is posted _before_ the ask returns, which is
what makes it a promise a caller can rely on: whoever holds an answer also knows the channel shows
it, and a test can assert the presence or the absence of the echo without waiting on a race. Its
failure is a warning and never the caller's error — the answer has arrived and a channel that could
not be written to must not take it away — which is why the refused-echo path is proved by a question
asked in a conversation the platform stops accepting (`C-once`) rather than by the happy path alone.
The text is built by `chatAnswerFormat` from the labels the person saw, because the stored answer is
machine-shaped on purpose.

### D-691 — Questions ask inline by default, with a form on request

> _2026-10-30 · realm/blong-chat · active_

A question is asked in the conversation unless the caller names `presentation: 'form'`, which is the
opposite of how the first pass worked. Inline on Slack is a radio group or a checkbox list in an
`actions` block plus a submit button under it; a free-text question has no field to show (a message
cannot carry one), so it says `reply here` and the pending question claims the next reply — the same
answer path Viber has always used. The form presentation stays because a modal is the only place
that puts options and a text box in one view, which is what `placeholder` is asking for. The reason
the default moved is that a dialog hides the question and the channel around it, and a question is
usually part of a conversation rather than an interruption of one. Two mechanisms make the inline
answer safe: a toggle is reported as its own interaction (`prompt.pick`, carrying the element's
whole selection) and is remembered against the waiting question, and the submit's `block_actions`
payload reports the message's state keyed by block — the submit answers with the state when it
arrives with one and with the remembered toggle when it does not, so a question is not silently
answered empty because Slack left the state out.

### D-692 — An answered question is rewritten in its own message

> _2026-10-30 · realm/blong-chat · active_

The answer is written over the question rather than announced beside it: once a question is answered
the message it was posted as is edited — options kept, the picked ones marked, the controls gone —
on Slack through `chat.update` and on Viber through `edit_message`. The reason is that a second
message cannot fix a control that is still on screen: the question carried a live button and a
submit that no longer did anything, and a reader had to reconcile two messages to learn what
happened. The cost is that an edit needs the platform's own id for the message, which is why the ask
keeps what its send reply named (`ts` on Slack, `message_token` on Viber) and why
`chatReplyMessageId` reads the two names; a platform that reports nothing falls back to posting the
answer as a message, and so does a refused edit. That fallback is the echo this replaced, kept
because it is the only thing left when an edit is impossible — and it is still a warning, never the
caller's error, because the answer has already arrived. `echoAnswer: false` therefore means "leave
the message alone", which is the one case where the stale controls stay.

### D-693 — A settled question names who answered, not what

> _2026-10-30 · realm/blong-chat · active_

The settled message names the person who answered instead of repeating the answer:
`🗨️ <@U1> answered`, which Slack renders with that user's avatar and name. The repetition was the
wrong half of the story — the marked options already say what was picked, while a reader of a group
conversation wants to know whose pick it was, and only the platform knows that. So the identity
travels on the answer (`IChatAnswer.sender`), filled by the port from the payload's `user` for every
interaction and not only for a form submission, and the router passes it through because the answer
is what gets shown back. Something typed is still appended (`answered: or maybe c`) since no mark
can carry it, a question with no options names its answer (`answered: Yes`), and an answer given by
a program — which has no identity — falls back to `_Answer:_ …` rather than to an empty greeting.
Viber has no mentions to render, so its edit writes the name out, and falls back to the word
`Answer` when there is none.

### D-716 — The ask takes the caller's prompt id when it has one

> _2026-10-31 · realm/blong-chat · active_

`chat.prompt.ask` now accepts an optional `promptId` from its caller and uses it instead of minting
one. A caller that checkpoints a pending question before asking has to record an id, and the answer
comes back quoting the prompt it answers: if the id is chat's own, the realm that asked is holding a
different one and a cold answer has nothing to attach to. Absent, the ask mints its own, which is
every other caller's behaviour and leaves their contract unchanged. The seam test in
`realm/blong-agent` is what found it — 46 chat tests stayed green, because inside one realm the id
is never compared across a boundary.

### D-725 — chat stores a channel binding and never learns what a persona is

> _2026-11-01 · realm/blong-chat · active_

A channel row keeps the platform, the account, the conversation id, the consumer method and a
binding of three generic columns: kind, key and a parameters json. What sits behind the binding is
the consumer decision, so a future binding to another realm carries its own parameters and this
realm needs no change. The agent side keeps the session truth, so the binding names the persona only
and the session is resolved from the channel key.

### D-727 — chat keeps its database optional through a channel store switch

> _2026-11-01 · realm/blong-chat · active_

The realm gains tables but must still run with no database, because its own test suite and a bare
listener deployment have none. The switch is `chat.chatDispatch.channelStore`, `none` by default, so
an inbound message is forwarded exactly as it is today, and a deployment that sets it to `db` gets
the lookup and the binding. The switch sits under the orchestrator slice because a handler reads the
config of the port it was dispatched on (@@F-641).

### D-796 — The chat portal and the chat webhooks answer on different hosts

> _2026-11-10 · realm/blong-chat · active_

The kustomize tree refuses a realm-contributed webhook path on a portal's host, because ingress
annotations belong to the host and a webhook would inherit the portal's authentication. The chat
deployment therefore names a host for the portal and another one for the Slack and Viber paths. The
portal host travels in the deployment rc file and the CR, as every address does; the webhook host
travels in the suite's own config, because the operator regenerates the tree from the artifact and
the CR has no field for a contributed ingress. Both hosts are named in the chat suite for this
deployment and a later pass that makes an ingress host tenant data moves the webhook address to the
CR.

### D-797 — The Slack configuration token belongs to the workspace, not the bot account

> _2026-11-10 · realm/blong-chat · active_

A Slack app configuration token authorizes app management in a workspace, so one pair serves every
bot account of that workspace. Storing it on the account row was wrong twice: two accounts of one
workspace would each try to renew the same pair and the first rotation spends the refresh token, and
a new account created through the portal would have to be handed the pair again. The pair therefore
lives in chat_workspace, an account names the workspace whose token maintains its app, and the port
groups accounts by workspace so a pass rotates once and applies the new pair to the whole group. The
account map a port reads still carries the resolved token fields, because the port should not have
to know where they are stored; the workspace alias travels beside them so the replacement is written
to the row it came from. App ids, the client id and the signing secret stay per account, because
each bot account is its own Slack app.

### D-802 — chat.prompt.ask requires auth, granted through chatManage

> _2026-11-10 · realm/blong-chat · active_

Asking a question is a message posted into a conversation, so the route answers to the same
authority as sending one: the gateway authenticates the caller and checks the `chat.prompt.ask`
action, which the realm's own seed grants through the `chatManage` capability, so a deployment needs
nothing extra beyond a re-run of its seeds. The first pass left the route open because the realm
carried no users and no access schema, and a caller's identity was nobody's question then; it is the
question now. The other three chat routes are still `auth: false` for that same obsolete reason and
are tracked separately. A test that cannot afford the access schema replaces the realm with
`blong-access-mock`, which is the feasible workaround — leaving a route open is not.

### D-806 — Channel creation needs channels:manage and groups:write

> _2026-11-11 · realm/blong-chat · active_

A bot that opens channels needs two scopes the chat realm did not ask for before: `channels:manage`
for a public channel and `groups:write` for a private one. Both are also what `conversations.invite`
and `conversations.setTopic` read, so a channel cannot be made useful with one without the other.

Slack does not report the gap as `missing_scope`. `conversations.create` answers
`ok: false, error: fatal_error`, which names neither the scope nor the call that needed it, so the
probe that found this had to compare the failure with the app's manifest. The manifest draft now
carries both scopes, so an app created from it works; an app that already exists keeps the scopes
its bot token was issued with, and adding a scope in the dashboard changes nothing until the app is
reinstalled and the new token is stored.

### D-805 — A plan's channel is opened by the chat realm

> _2026-11-11 · realm/blong-chat · active_

A channel a plan owns is opened by the chat realm, not by the tooling that asks for it. The platform
credential lives in a deployment's account store, so `blong-dev` can name a channel but cannot
authenticate one; `chat.channel.create` is the method it calls, and the realm is what reaches the
port.

The port makes the four Slack calls a channel needs — `conversations.create`,
`conversations.setPurpose`, `conversations.setTopic` and `conversations.invite` — and the realm owns
their order and the bookkeeping. The purpose carries the plan's readable title, because a channel
name is lowercase and hyphenated and the title does not survive in it; the topic carries the GitHub
issue, so the two halves of the channel say which plan it is and where its record is. Both follow
the create because Slack has no creation parameter for either, the invite follows because a private
channel has no members, and the channel row is written last so a failed create leaves no half-met
conversation. Private is the default because unfinished work is not a workspace announcement; the
caller names the user ids to add.

The id is stored by the caller, not by this realm. A plan keeps its `conversationId` in its own
file, which is also what `chat.prompt.ask` addresses, so a second approval run skips the create
instead of opening a twin. A name Slack already holds answers `name_taken`, which the realm reports
as a typed failure rather than resolving by searching: the caller that created the channel is the
one that has its id.

### D-820 — A free-text question is asked as a card, not a reply

> _2026-11-11 · realm/blong-chat · active_

The inline free-text question failed live in the plan channel and worked in a public one, which
pointed at the private channel rather than at the realm. Two separate settings were missing and both
had to be there: a plan's channel is created private, Slack delivers its messages as message.groups,
and that needs the groups:history scope; and Slack tells an app about an event only if the app
subscribed to it, which the manifest did not for the private case. The app's event subscription was
in place for public channels, so the fault looked like a scope alone and was not. With the scope
granted and the port subscribing the events (D-821), a reply in a private plan channel answers an
inline question, proved live. The card stays the default because it needs no event at all and
answers in one payload, and inline stays the choice for a message that wants no typing; the earlier
rule against pinning a text question to inline is withdrawn, and the caveat that remains is a
deployment whose app was installed by hand without those two settings.

### D-822 — A parked question may wait three days, and a restart loses it

> _2026-11-11 · realm/blong-chat · active_

A question that may wait for days is still asked as a blocking chat.prompt.ask, and losing the
answer to a restart is accepted rather than designed around: the caller re-asks, which costs one
message and no bookkeeping. Three days is the horizon worth supporting, so the client keeps its
connection open for the life of the wait and the server accepts a timeoutMs up to 2147483647 ms, the
point where setTimeout saturates and a longer delay would fire as soon as it was scheduled; above
the ceiling the ask refuses with chat.promptTimeoutTooLong instead of reporting a closure that
already happened, and the label on the closed message speaks in days and hours so a three-day wait
does not read as thousands of minutes. The durable shape stays where it already was:
agent.question.ask checkpoints before it asks and treats its timeout as a suspension, so a question
that must survive anything belongs there and not in the port.

## Superseded

### D-795 — A Slack config token is a rotating pair the realm stores

> _2026-11-10 · realm/blong-chat · superseded_

A Slack app configuration token expires, and rotating it returns a new access token _and_ a new
refresh token, so the old refresh token stops working the moment it is spent. The port therefore
rotates only what it can persist: it dispatches chat.account.provision with the new pair, and
without a save method it leaves the pair alone rather than spending a rotation the next restart
cannot see. Accounts come from chat.account.list when the database holds any, and that map replaces
the configured one rather than merging with it, because two sources of one credential is the state a
person cannot reason about. The same method carries what app creation returned, which is why it is
named provision rather than rotate.

the token pair is workspace-scoped, not account-scoped

Superseded by `D-797`.
